result: Inhba and Fst are expressed in opposing gradients within the developing cochlea that correlate with the spatial and temporal pattern of hair cell differentiation. At E13.5, Inhba expression is limited to the basal pro-sensory domain where Atoh1 expression begins, while Fst is highly expressed in the apex and mid-turn but weakly in the base. As differentiation progresses (E14.5-E15.5), Inhba expression extends apically while Fst expression regresses basally, creating a counter-gradient that parallels the basal-to-apical wave of hair cell differentiation.
evaluation: Claims C29-C34 are well-supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figures 1A-C demonstrating the opposing expression gradients of Inhba and Fst across developmental stages. The spatial and temporal correlation between these gradients and Atoh1 expression provides strong evidence for the proposed relationship, though the inference in C34 about pro-sensory cells being exposed to an Activin A signaling gradient is reasonable but indirect.

result: Exogenous Activin A treatment promotes precocious hair cell differentiation in E13.5 cochlear explants. After 12 hours of Activin A treatment, GFP-positive inner hair cells are evident in treated explants but not controls, and the band of differentiated cells extends further apically at all time points examined. Activin A treatment increases expression of hair cell markers (Atoh1 >4-fold, Lgr5 >4-fold, Pou4f3 >12-fold) and decreases expression of differentiation inhibitors (Bmp4, Id2, Id3, Id4 >2-fold reduction) without affecting other pro-sensory genes.
evaluation: Claims C36-C43 are strongly supported by experimental data from cochlear explant cultures (Figure 2B-D) showing both morphological evidence of precocious differentiation and quantitative RT-qPCR data demonstrating specific transcriptional changes. The consistency between the morphological observations and molecular changes provides converging evidence for Activin A's pro-differentiation role.

result: Activin A and BMP4 have distinct effects on Id gene expression and activate different SMAD pathways in the developing cochlea. Brief BMP4 treatment increases Id1 and Id3 expression but not Id4 or Atoh1, while brief Activin A treatment modestly decreases Id4 expression without affecting Id1-3 or Atoh1. Activin A selectively stimulates SMAD2/3 phosphorylation while BMP4 selectively induces SMAD1/5/9 phosphorylation, suggesting Activin A regulates Atoh1 indirectly through repression of Id gene expression.
evaluation: Claims C45-C49 are supported by RT-qPCR data (Figure 2F) and Western blot analysis (Figure 2G) demonstrating differential responses to Activin A versus BMP4 treatment. The selective SMAD phosphorylation patterns confirm distinct signaling pathways. However, the mechanistic inference in C49 about indirect regulation is reasonable but not definitively proven by these data alone.

result: FST overexpression delays hair cell differentiation and antagonizes Activin signaling in the developing cochlea. At E14.5, FST overexpressing cochlear tissue lacks hair cells present in controls, shows reduced Atoh1 and Pou4f3 expression, and increased Id3 and Id4 expression. FST overexpression significantly reduces P-SMAD2/3 protein levels (indicating reduced Activin signaling) but does not affect P-SMAD1/5/9 levels (indicating intact BMP signaling).
evaluation: Claims C50-C58 are well-supported by multiple lines of evidence including morphological analysis (Figures 3C-D), RT-qPCR data (Figure 3E), and Western blot analysis (Figures 3F-G). The selective reduction in P-SMAD2/3 without affecting P-SMAD1/5/9 provides strong evidence that FST specifically antagonizes Activin signaling without disrupting BMP signaling in this context.

result: Activin A rescues the FST-mediated delay in hair cell differentiation in cochlear explants. Hair cell differentiation occurs significantly earlier in Activin A-treated wild type explants compared to untreated controls, while FST overexpression significantly delays differentiation. When Activin A treatment is combined with FST overexpression, the delay is almost completely abolished, with no significant differences compared to wild type untreated explants.
evaluation: Claims C59-C62 are strongly supported by experimental data from cochlear explant rescue experiments (Figures 4B-F). The ability of Activin A to rescue FST-mediated delays provides compelling evidence that FST antagonizes hair cell differentiation in an Activin A-dependent manner, though other Activin-type ligands may also be involved.

result: FST overexpression (induced at E11.5) causes ectopic inner hair cell formation and severe delays in cochlear differentiation/maturation. At E18.5, R26-FST cochlear tissue contains two rows of inner hair cells throughout the basal half (instead of one row), with correspondingly increased inner phalangeal cell density. The auditory sensory epithelium is 30% shorter than controls, hair cells have less mature stereocilia, and apical hair cells lack stereocilia completely.
evaluation: Claims C64-C70 are well-supported by morphological analysis and quantitative measurements (Figures 5A-D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1). The observation that inner phalangeal cell density also increases (C65) provides important evidence against a supporting cell-to-hair cell conversion mechanism. The multiple phenotypic abnormalities are consistent and statistically significant.

result: FST induction at E13.0 (one day later than E11.5) does not affect cochlear length but still causes ectopic inner hair cell formation and delayed hair cell maturation. The length of the auditory sensory epithelium at E17.5 is not significantly different from controls, but ectopic inner hair cells are observed (highest number in the basal portion), and hair cell stereocilia have a less mature phenotype compared to controls.
evaluation: Claims C71-C73 are supported by experimental measurements and morphological analysis (Figures 6A-B). The temporal specificity of the phenotype (affecting patterning and maturation but not length when induced later) provides important information about the critical windows for FST action, though sample size for length measurement is modest (n=3).

result: Conditional knockout of Inhba (Activin A) results in hair cell maturation and patterning defects similar to but milder than FST overexpression. Inhba cKO does not alter overall cochlear morphology or sensory epithelium length at P0, but shows a significant increase in ectopic inner hair cells (concentrated in the basal segment) and less mature hair cell stereocilia throughout the cochlea compared to controls.
evaluation: Claims C74-C78 are supported by experimental data from Inhba conditional knockout mice (Figures 6C-D). The milder phenotype compared to FST overexpression suggests FST may target additional Activin-type ligands beyond Activin A. However, the sample size for length measurement is small (n=2), which limits confidence in the statistical conclusion about unchanged length.

result: FST likely disrupts multiple Activin-related signaling mechanisms beyond Activin A in the developing cochlea. The milder defects in Inhba mutants compared to FST transgenic animals suggest additional targets. GDF11 is identified as the predominant Activin-type ligand in the developing cochlea based on RT-qPCR analysis, while Inhbb and Mstn are expressed at very low or undetectable levels.
evaluation: Claims C79-C82 and C118 are supported by comparative phenotypic analysis and RT-qPCR expression data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1). The inference that FST targets additional ligands beyond Activin A is reasonable given the phenotypic differences, and GDF11 is a plausible candidate based on its high expression and known FST binding. However, functional validation of GDF11's role would strengthen this conclusion.

result: FST overexpression delays pro-sensory cell cycle withdrawal along the longitudinal cochlear axis but does not disrupt the apical-to-basal gradient. When EdU is administered at E13.5 and analyzed at E18.5, basal hair cells incorporate EdU at similar rates (~25%) in both control and FST overexpressing animals, but mid and apical hair cells in FST overexpressing cochleae show robust EdU incorporation while controls show little to none. Apical hair cells still incorporate EdU at lower rates than basal hair cells in FST tissue, indicating the gradient is preserved.
evaluation: Claims C84-C87 are well-supported by EdU incorporation data (Figures 7A-E). The preservation of the apical-to-basal gradient despite delayed cell cycle exit is an important observation that distinguishes effects on timing from effects on spatial patterning. The data clearly demonstrate region-specific effects of FST overexpression.

result: A medial-to-lateral gradient of terminal mitosis exists in wild type cochlear tissue, with inner hair cell progenitors withdrawing from the cell cycle prior to outer hair cell progenitors. In the mid-turn of control cochleae, more than 6% of outer hair cells are EdU-positive while no inner hair cells incorporate EdU. This distinct medial-to-lateral gradient is lost in FST overexpressing cochlear tissue, where inner and outer hair cells incorporate EdU at similar rates.
evaluation: Claims C88-C89 and C128-C129 are supported by EdU incorporation data (Figures 7D-E, 8E-F) demonstrating a previously unrecognized radial gradient of cell cycle exit. This is a novel finding with important implications for understanding hair cell production. The loss of this gradient in FST overexpressing tissue provides mechanistic insight into the ectopic inner hair cell phenotype.

result: Prolonged EdU labeling (E14.5-E17.5) reveals that FST overexpression causes prolonged proliferation of inner hair cell progenitors. Supporting cells and hair cells in R26-FST animals incorporate EdU at much higher frequency than controls. In control tissue, outer hair cells (12.1%) incorporate EdU at significantly higher rates than inner hair cells (1.5%), but in FST tissue inner hair cells incorporate EdU at similar or higher rates than outer hair cells. In the apex of FST tissue, only inner hair cells and inner phalangeal cells are EdU-labeled.
evaluation: Claims C90-C94 are strongly supported by EdU incorporation data from prolonged labeling experiments (Figures 8A-F). The specific labeling of inner hair cells and inner phalangeal cells in the apex of FST tissue (C93) provides particularly compelling evidence that ectopic inner hair cells arise from prolonged proliferation rather than fate conversion. The inference in C94 is well-justified by the data.

result: At the peak of terminal mitosis (E13.5), Fst expression becomes restricted to the lateral portion of the pro-sensory domain, suggesting inner hair cell progenitors experience higher levels of Activin-type signaling than outer hair cell progenitors. This radial gradient of Activin signaling constitutes a novel mechanism for limiting the number of inner hair cells produced in the mammalian cochlea.
evaluation: Claims C130-C132 are supported by in situ hybridization data (Figure 1A) and the functional data demonstrating differential cell cycle exit timing. The inference in C131 about differential Activin-type signaling exposure is reasonable based on the expression patterns. The conclusion in C132 about a novel mechanism is justified by the combination of expression data and functional experiments, though the term 'novel' should be interpreted in the context of this specific system.

result: A local gradient of Activin A signaling within the auditory sensory epithelium times the longitudinal gradient of hair cell differentiation, and Activin-type signaling regulates a radial gradient of terminal mitosis that limits inner hair cell production. Activin A acts as a pro-differentiation signal, as demonstrated by exogenous Activin A triggering premature differentiation in explants and disruption of Activin A signaling (via FST overexpression or Inhba deletion) causing delayed differentiation in vivo.
evaluation: Claims C4, C5, and C95 represent the main conclusions of the manuscript and are well-supported by the comprehensive experimental evidence including expression analysis, gain-of-function (FST overexpression), loss-of-function (Inhba deletion), and rescue experiments. The combination of longitudinal and radial gradients provides a sophisticated model for how Activin signaling controls both timing and number of hair cells produced.

result: Activin signaling does not directly activate Atoh1 expression or interfere with SHH signaling, but rather acts indirectly through inhibition of Id3 and Id4 expression. Brief (4 hr) Activin A treatment does not significantly increase Atoh1 transcript, and neither over-activation nor loss of Activin signaling alters expression of SHH target genes (Hey1, Hey2, Fgf20). The authors propose a model where Wnt/β-catenin signaling initiates Atoh1 expression while Activin signaling enhances it along the longitudinal axis.
evaluation: Claims C97-C99, C101, and C103 are supported by experimental data showing no changes in SHH target genes and no immediate Atoh1 response to brief Activin treatment. The indirect mechanism through Id gene repression is well-supported. However, the proposed model in C103 integrating Wnt and Activin signaling is speculative and based on inference from the current data combined with prior literature rather than direct experimental validation in this study.

result: FST overexpression delays pro-sensory cell cycle withdrawal and differentiation through mechanisms that may involve p27/Kip1 protein stability/activity and increased Id3/Id4 expression. The expression pattern of Fst mimics that of Lin28b (both highly expressed in pro-sensory cells and downregulated following a basal-to-apical gradient). No changes in p27/Kip1 mRNA are observed with FST overexpression, suggesting effects on protein level rather than transcription.
evaluation: Claims C107-C109 are supported by experimental data, but C112-C114 involve speculative mechanisms. The lack of p27/Kip1 mRNA changes (C112) is documented, but the inference about protein stability/activity (C113) and the contribution of increased Id3/Id4 (C114) are reasonable hypotheses that lack direct experimental validation. The comparison to Lin28b (C108-C109) is interesting but does not establish a functional connection.

result: FST overexpression and Inhba ablation result in overproduction of inner hair cells through prolonged progenitor proliferation rather than disruption of BMP signaling or fate conversion. FST overexpression does not disrupt or significantly reduce BMP signaling (unchanged P-SMAD1/5/9 levels and Id1-3 expression), and the increased inner phalangeal cell density argues against supporting cell-to-hair cell conversion.
evaluation: Claims C122-C123 and C126-C127 are supported by experimental data showing ectopic inner hair cells, intact BMP signaling markers, and increased supporting cell density. The inference in C127 about prolonged proliferation is well-supported by the EdU incorporation data. The exclusion of alternative mechanisms (BMP disruption, fate conversion) strengthens the proposed mechanism.

result: The mammalian auditory sensory epithelium has a highly stereotyped cellular pattern with precise rows of hair cells (one row of inner and three rows of outer hair cells). Differentiation is precisely timed and follows opposing gradients: pro-sensory cells exit the cell cycle in an apical-to-basal gradient while hair cell differentiation occurs in a basal-to-apical gradient. A shallower medial-to-lateral gradient also exists, with inner hair cells differentiating before outer hair cells.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C6-C7, and C135-C136 represent established knowledge in the field supported by citations to previous studies and confirmed by observations in this manuscript. These claims provide essential background context for understanding the experimental findings but are not novel contributions of this work.

result: Prior work has established that SHH signaling from spiral ganglion neurons represses hair cell differentiation through maintaining HEY1/HEY2 expression, which antagonizes ATOH1 function. ID proteins downstream of BMP signaling also maintain pro-sensory cells in an undifferentiated state by interfering with ATOH1. Wnt/β-catenin signaling is required for hair cell formation but its activity pattern does not parallel the differentiation gradient. Inhba is expressed in a basal-to-apical gradient in the differentiating cochlea.
evaluation: Claims C8-C23 summarize established knowledge from prior studies (supported by citations) that provides the scientific context for the current work. These claims accurately represent the state of the field and identify the gap (lack of understanding about pro-differentiation signals) that this study addresses. They are not novel findings but essential background.

result: Activins belong to the TGF-β superfamily and control diverse biological processes. Canonical TGF-β signaling is transduced by R-SMADs that form complexes with SMAD4 to activate target genes. FST antagonizes Activin signaling by encircling the Inhibin β dimer and blocking receptor binding. In the developing spinal cord, Activins are required for Atoh1 induction in neuronal progenitors. Within the differentiating auditory sensory epithelium, Fst and Inhba are expressed in opposing gradients.
evaluation: Claims C24-C28, C35, C133-C134 represent established knowledge about Activin/TGF-β signaling mechanisms and FST function, supported by citations to previous studies. Claim C134 about opposing gradients in the cochlea is supported by prior work (Son et al., 2015) and confirmed by data in this manuscript. These provide essential mechanistic context but are not novel findings.

result: Prior work has established various aspects of signaling pathway regulation in cochlear development and other systems: BMP signaling regulates Id1-3 expression; failure to downregulate Id3 inhibits hair cell formation; Wnt/β-catenin is required for hair cell specification; early SHH signaling establishes regional identity; Notch signaling regulates Inhba expression; TGF-β pathways inhibit proliferation through CDK inhibitors; p27/Kip1 regulates pro-sensory cell cycle exit; ID proteins are associated with proliferative states; FST can be detected early in otocyst development; GDF11-FST axis regulates progenitor cells in other sensory tissues; Activin signaling has different effects in chicken versus mammalian auditory epithelia; FST can interfere with BMP signaling in some tissues; BMP signaling is critical for cochlear patterning.
evaluation: Claims C44, C100, C102, C104-C106, C110-C111, C115-C116, C119-C121, C124-C125 represent established knowledge from prior studies (all supported by citations) that provides context for interpreting the current findings. These claims accurately represent relevant background information but are not novel contributions of this work.

result: Induction of FST overexpression at E11.5 or E14.5 results in neonatal lethality of R26-FST transgenic animals, limiting analysis to late embryonic stages.
evaluation: Claim C63 is a straightforward observation about the experimental system that is important for understanding the limitations of the study. This is a technical constraint rather than a scientific finding, but it is clearly documented and affects the interpretation of results.

result: In the developing cortex, Activin signaling promotes interneuron differentiation through inhibition of SHH signaling.
evaluation: Claim C96 is supported by a citation to previous work (Cambray et al., 2012) and is used as a comparison point to discuss potential mechanisms in the cochlea. This is background information from another system rather than a finding of the current study.
